stat.l: main code words, from detonation to deficiency

lines.text: NUCFLASH.
This is the top of the ladder: a possible, or actual, nuclear detonation, or any event, like an accidental missile launch, that could create the risk of a nuclear war.
Its report goes out with the highest precedence in the military's incident reporting system.
And as far as the public record shows, the United States has never had an accidental nuclear explosion.
Broken Arrow.
A Broken Arrow is an accident involving a nuclear weapon that does not create a risk of nuclear war.
The Pentagon's official list counts thirty-two of them between nineteen fifty and nineteen eighty.
In nineteen fifty-eight, after a mid-air collision on a training flight, a B-47 bomber jettisoned a nuclear weapon near Tybee Island, off the coast of Georgia.
After ten weeks of searching, it was declared lost. It has never been recovered.
In nineteen sixty-one, a B-52 broke apart near Goldsboro, North Carolina, and two bombs fell.
Exactly how close one of them came to detonating is still debated today.
In nineteen sixty-six, a B-52 collided with its refueling tanker off the coast near Palomares, Spain, and four hydrogen bombs fell.
Three landed near the village.
The fourth fell into the sea, and was recovered about eighty days later, with help from a local fisherman who had seen where it went down.
In nineteen sixty-eight, a B-52 with a fire on board crashed near Thule Air Base in Greenland, and its weapons broke apart, scattering radioactive material across the ice.
And in nineteen eighty, in Damascus, Arkansas, a dropped socket punctured the fuel tank of a Titan Two missile in its silo.
The fuel exploded. The warhead did not.
Empty Quiver.
Empty Quiver means a working nuclear weapon has been seized, stolen, or lost.
It's the scenario security systems are built around.
And there's no publicly confirmed case of an American nuclear weapon being stolen.
Bent Spear.
A Bent Spear is a significant incident involving nuclear weapons that falls short of a Broken Arrow.
The best known one happened in two thousand seven.
A B-52 flew from Minot Air Force Base to Barksdale in Louisiana, carrying six cruise missiles that still had their nuclear warheads.
The warheads were supposed to have been removed.
The crew's preflight check looked at only one wing's missiles, the ones without warheads.
They sat on the bomber for about thirty-six hours before anyone realized.
The Air Force called it a series of procedural breakdowns and human errors.
Commanders were relieved, and the Air Force said seventy airmen would be disciplined.
Faded Giant.
Faded Giant covers a different kind of event: an accident with a military nuclear reactor, or another radiological accident that doesn't involve a weapon.
That's why it gets its own word.
The ladder doesn't only track bombs.
Dull Sword.
Dull Sword is the bottom rung: a safety deficiency, or a minor problem with a nuclear weapon, its parts, or the equipment built to handle it.
It sounds small, but reporting the small problems is how the big ones are prevented.
One more word sits on top of the ladder: Pinnacle.
Pinnacle marks the reports that go straight to the National Military Command Center at the Pentagon, like Pinnacle NUCFLASH, Pinnacle Broken Arrow, and Pinnacle Empty Quiver.
So, from the top. NUCFLASH, a detonation. Broken Arrow, an accident. Empty Quiver, a missing weapon. Bent Spear, an incident. Faded Giant, a reactor. And Dull Sword, a deficiency.
Which of these surprised you most? Tell me in the comments.
